title: Anil Menon Completes NASA's 100th US Spacewalk, Installing Seventh ISS Solar Array
excerpt: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canada's Joshua Kutryk spent 7 hours 11 minutes outside the International Space Station on October 29, deploying the seventh roll-out solar array in the station's power upgrade.
body:
• NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk on October 29, installing the seventh roll-out solar array on the International Space Station.
  • The excursion was the 100th US spacewalk conducted from the station's Quest airlock and the 285th spacewalk in support of the ISS overall.
  • Once the eighth and final array is installed on November 5, the upgrade will raise the station's available power by up to 30 percent, from about 160 to roughly 215 kilowatts.
  • It was Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first — the first by a Canadian astronaut since 2019.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk completed the 100th US spacewalk from the International Space Station on Thursday, spending 7 hours and 11 minutes outside the orbiting laboratory to install and deploy its seventh roll-out solar array, according to NASA. The pair exited the station's Quest airlock at 7:57 a.m. EDT and ended the spacewalk at 3:08 p.m. EDT.

What the spacewalkers did

Menon, wearing a suit with red stripes as crew member 1, rode the Canadarm2 robotic arm to carry the 750-pound (340-kilogram) International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array, or iROSA, to the station's port-side truss, where the pair installed it on the 2A electrical power channel. The array, delivered earlier this month inside the trunk of a SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule on the company's 35th resupply mission, unrolled to its full 63-foot length without a motor, driven by the stored energy in its composite booms. The astronauts also completed preparatory tasks for the final array installation.

Why the power upgrade matters

The station's eight original solar arrays have exceeded their 15-year design life and are producing less power than they once did. The eight iROSA blankets are being layered over the older wings to restore and expand capacity. NASA says the completed upgrade will increase available power by up to 30 percent, supporting critical station operations through the laboratory's remaining service life, including its safe and controlled deorbit, currently planned around 2030.

Part of a longer upgrade campaign

The roll-out arrays, built with solar cells mounted on flexible blankets that unfurl like a rug, are designed to be lighter and more compact than the rigid panels they supplement. Six iROSAs were installed between 2021 and 2023; this week's pair of spacewalks finishes the set. Thursday's excursion was the 285th spacewalk devoted to station assembly, maintenance and upgrades overall, a tally that also includes 66 excursions from the station's Russian segment and 119 conducted by visiting space shuttle crews.

A milestone for both astronauts

The outing was Menon's fourth spacewalk. For Kutryk it was the first, making him only the fifth Canadian astronaut to walk in space and the first to do so since David Saint-Jacques in April 2019. Inside the station, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney supported the excursion, including operating the Canadarm2 arm that moved Menon and the array into position.

What happens next

Menon and Kutryk are scheduled to go out again on Thursday, November 5, for US spacewalk 101, to install the eighth and final iROSA on the station's 3B power channel. That excursion will complete a power-augmentation programme that began in 2021 and close out the station's last major upgrade before its planned retirement at the end of the decade.
